A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Tibetan corpus and Qwen2.5 adaptation project, with v5 extending it to mixture-of-experts models. Their complete main texts, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison despite renaming, relocation and removal of material.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations in Tables 2–3, long-context retrieval results in Appendix F/Figure 1, tokenizer measurements in Appendix J, and generated examples in Appendix K.

after.justification: V5 retains the original dense-model evaluations and reports additional MoE benchmark results in Table 3 and an initialization comparison in Section 6.3.

M1.justification: V5 Section 6 adds a 50B-parameter MoE model with approximately 10B active parameters. It upcycles the Tibetan-adapted dense checkpoint, replaces alternating feed-forward layers with 16-expert layers using Top-2 routing, and applies further pre-training and instruction tuning. The original dense-model pipeline remains.

E1.justification: V5 adds training material from Tibetan PDFs and Chinese texts concerning Tibet. The six quantitative benchmarks and bilingual long-context retrieval scenarios remain unchanged. V1 Appendix K's qualitative demonstrations of literary translation, sentiment classification, poetry and coding are removed, modestly narrowing demonstrated task coverage.

E2.justification: The baseline sets in corresponding benchmark tables and tokenizer comparisons remain unchanged. V5 Section 6.3 adds a comparison between MoE initialization directly from Qwen2.5-7B-base and initialization from the Tibetan-adapted checkpoint; its outcome is reported qualitatively.

E3.justification: The added MoE experiments introduce a substantially larger model, a 40.7B-token pre-training stage at 4K context, an 8K context-extension stage, and an initialization control. V5 Appendix C also changes several reported filtering units from lines to sentences. These are reported protocol changes; rerunning the retained dense experiments is not established.

E4.justification: V5 Section 6.3 adds a qualitative initialization ablation testing whether Tibetan adaptation before MoE upcycling matters. V1 Appendix K's five generation examples disappear. The existing long-context and tokenizer analyses are retained in Sections 7.5–7.6, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and retrieval heatmaps without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or statistical significance tests. The added MoE results follow the same reporting practice.

E6.justification: V5 Table 3 adds results for three MoE variants; MoE-SFT reports 53.67 ARC accuracy, 72.96 XStoryCloze accuracy and 74.37 TibetanQA F1. These involve different model capacity and additional training data. Every retained comparison-table row, all eight retrieval heatmaps and the tokenizer measurements are unchanged. The five qualitative generation outputs are removed.

T1.justification: Neither version presents theoretical propositions, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations. V5's characters-per-token explanation clarifies the existing compression metric; its MoE reasoning remains architectural and qualitative.

C1.justification: V1 centers its contributions on the Tibetan corpus, benchmarks and dense Banzhida model. V5's abstract, introduction and conclusion expand the contribution to dense and MoE models, claiming efficient capacity scaling through initialization from a Tibetan-adapted checkpoint and transferable insights for other low-resource languages.

C2.justification: V5 adds explanations involving fragmented expert representations and instruction tuning unlocking MoE capacity. Its limitations replace v1's emphasis on unavailable PDF-derived data and restricted model scale with substantive concerns about domain and dialect coverage, translation artifacts, cultural validity of translated benchmarks, and unresolved expert-routing and efficiency tradeoffs.

D1.justification: V5 discloses instruction-data counts and MoE initialization details, but removes v1 Tables 5–9 identifying collected corpora, crawl domains and counts, filtering terms, long-context sources, and instruction-data links. Dense-model hardware and optimization details remain. V5 promises future artifact releases without supplying access links, and reports 55 crawled sites in Section 3.1 versus 45 in Appendix B.

R1.justification: V5 expands the research positioning to sparse MoE scaling and dense-to-MoE upcycling, adding work by Shazeer, Fedus, He, Hui, Liew and others. Several data-source references disappear with the removed provenance tables. Updates to Qwen, TiLamb and other retained references are bibliographic changes rather than new research connections.

P1.justification: V5 rewrites the title, abstract, conclusion and limitations, changes author information and model naming, and reorganizes the narrative around dense and MoE training. Corpus composition, long-context analysis and tokenizer analysis move into the main text; the appendices are substantially condensed and the generation-example section is removed.

P2.justification: V5 adds training-flow and architecture diagrams, expands and regroups the main comparison table, and moves the unchanged retrieval heatmaps into the main text as Figure 3. V1 Table 4 becomes main-text Table 1, while Tables 5–9 and the five boxed generation examples are removed.

improvement.justification: V5 adds meaningful scaling results, clearer architectural diagrams and substantially better discussion of limitations. However, deleting v1 Tables 5–9 materially weakens reproducibility of the central data-curation contribution. The new initialization advantage is only qualitative, and MoE efficiency claims lack direct cost measurements. These gains and losses, together with inconsistent crawl documentation, leave the net change in overall quality uncertain.
